characters: Maku: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform, with a notebook and a thoughtful look.
Grandma Oforiwaa: an elderly woman in a cloth and head tie, sweeping with a bundle of broom sticks; she did not go to school.
Uncle Idris: Maku’s uncle, an engineer in a smart shirt and sunglasses, driving a car.
Auntie Pamela: Maku’s aunt, a lawyer in a neat dress, with a folder of papers.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, wry grandmother’s voice for Grandma Oforiwaa; thoughtful girl’s voice for Maku; a gentle, embarrassed uncle
narrationPlan.pace: Warm and thoughtful, with a smile for the grandmother (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Warm, gentle highlife guitar with a slow steady beat; a quiet pause at the car window (placeholder)
culturalNotes: This story gives several honest reasons: law, health, faith, neighbours, fairness and money. It does not say that any religion or culture was wrong to teach children about cleanliness; it says children deserve true and complete reasons.
Scripture and sayings are paraphrased and should be checked by a pastor or imam. Families of all faiths and none should feel respected.
Grandma’s old story about a spirit in the gutter is an invented example of a frightening reason that is not true, not a claim about any real belief.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: Public Health Act 2012 (Act 851) section 56 offence; the Lapaz case in 2017 (21 people fined GH¢720 each or six months in jail); cholera June 2014 to February 2015 (over 20,500 cases, 121 deaths; breakdown in waste management); World Bank flood-loss estimate (not used here).
Have a pastor, an imam and a traditional leader review the faith paragraph (Genesis 2:15; Deuteronomy 23:12 to 14; the saying that cleanliness is half of faith; Qur’an 7:56; Leviticus 19:18).
The fines mentioned are from 2017 and may have changed; the story says so. Check current rules with the Environmental Health service.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about giving children true, many-sided reasons for a good habit. It shows an educated person who litters and an unschooled elder who keeps her street clean, and it breaks the idea that care for the environment depends on certificates.
learningGoals: List at least four true reasons not to dump rubbish: law, health, faith, neighbours and fairness.
Explain why true reasons are better than scary stories.
Say how an adult can model good behaviour.
beforeReading: Ask: have you ever been told a scary reason for a rule? Did it work for ever?
whileReading: At page 6, invite learners of different faiths to share, if they wish, a teaching on cleanliness from their tradition.
afterReading: Interview a grandparent about how they kept their street clean.
discussion: Why does the story say that rubbish does not read?
Why do true reasons last longer than scary stories?
reflection: Which reason moves you most, and why?

mathsExtension.task: 21 people were fined GH¢720 each. What was the total?
Cholera: over 20,500 cases and 121 deaths. About how many cases for each death? (Round to the nearest whole number.)

support: Give learners a chart with columns for Law, Health, Faith, Neighbours.
stretch: Find one other country’s fine for littering and compare it with Ghana’s.

culturalNotes: This story gives several honest reasons: law, health, faith, neighbours, fairness and money. It does not say that any religion or culture was wrong to teach children about cleanliness; it says children deserve true and complete reasons.
Scripture and sayings are paraphrased and should be checked by a pastor or imam. Families of all faiths and none should feel respected.
Grandma’s old story about a spirit in the gutter is an invented example of a frightening reason that is not true, not a claim about any real belief.
localiseThis: Invite faith leaders and traditional leaders to share their teachings, and let families speak for their own beliefs.

factCheck.claim: Twenty-one people were each fined GH¢720 (or six months in jail if unpaid) at Abeka District Court under section 56(a) and (b) of the Public Health Act, 2012 (Act 851) for dumping refuse in unauthorised areas; officials called it a cholera risk.
factCheck.explanation: From a Daily Graphic report published 23 July 2017.
factCheck.reference: Daily Graphic, “Twenty-one Lapaz residents fined GH¢15,120 for indiscriminate dumping of refuse”.

factCheck.claim: More than 20,500 cholera cases and 121 deaths were recorded in Greater Accra between June 2014 and February 2015; a doctor attributed the high case count to a breakdown in waste management.
factCheck.explanation: From a Graphic Online report of 19 March 2015.
factCheck.reference: Graphic Online, “Accra recorded 20,500 cholera cases between June 2014 and Feb 2015”.

factCheck.claim: Genesis 2:15 (to work the garden and take care of it); Deuteronomy 23:12 to 14 (a place outside the camp for waste, to be covered); Leviticus 19:18 (love your neighbour as yourself); a saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad that cleanliness is half of faith (Sahih Muslim); Qur’an 7:56 (do not spread corruption on the earth).
factCheck.explanation: Standard religious texts. The story paraphrases them, and a faith leader should confirm the wording.
factCheck.reference: The Bible; Sahih Muslim; the Qur’an. Review by a pastor and an imam recommended.

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).
